"Fair. Turning back is yours and Quell's. Stopping is mine. That's a split I can live with." He scoops the silver and copper off the table into his purse. "And I'll settle the money with Quell myself, like you say."

He stands and stretches until his back cracks, then glances down at the water cup under Garrick's hand.

"One thing, Sergeant, and then I'll leave it. I made my living for ten years watching men's hands across a table. Yours goes to that cup every time you talk about the men who didn't come back, and it stays there." He says it lightly, without any edge. "Maybe that's grief. I've seen that tell on honest men too. But if one of those seven guards was yours, or you sent somebody on that run who shouldn't have gone, I'd rather hear it from you on the road than work it out at the ford."

He doesn't wait for an answer. He swings the cloak straight on his shoulders.

"We'll go now, before the second bell. I'd like to see the yard while it's just Ambry and the loaders, before the man paying for it walks in and everyone stands up straighter."

He clicks his tongue softly toward the hearth. *Come on, your ladyship. Work.* On the way to the door he catches Tobin's eye across the room and gives him a small nod that says *keep watching*.

*(Out of game: if Garrick's answer about the cup is something James would read with Insight, I'll roll it. I'm not proficient, so it's Wisdom +1.)*
turns.reply:
Garrick doesn't move while James talks. The hand on the cup stays where it is. He doesn't pull it away when it's named either, and that tells James something by itself. He just looks at it, as if it belonged to another man.

James watches him for the answer under the answer, the way he used to watch a man deciding whether to call. He doesn't get it. Garrick's face goes still and stays like that, a sergeant's face on parade, and whatever is behind it stays there. It might be grief, guilt, or just an old soldier who doesn't like being read in a common room. From across a breakfast table James can't tell which, and it bothers him a little that he can't.

Garrick takes his hand off the cup and lays it flat on the table beside the other.

"On the road," he says. That's all. It isn't a yes, and it isn't a denial.

He plants his right boot, gets the stiff leg out from under the table and stands. The sword goes onto his belt properly this time, the buckle drawn tight with a tug. He looks at the cup once more before he leaves it.

"Now suits. Ambry'll be at the gate by this hour. Quell keeps a strict book, and the boy keeps it stricter."

By the hearth there's a small scrape of claws on stone. The cat comes out from among the ash buckets, stops to stretch one back leg as if it were her own idea, and pads after James. She goes past Garrick's boots close enough to brush them. He looks down at her, then at James, and says nothing about it.

Tobin is wiping a table that doesn't need wiping. He catches the nod and gives a very serious one back, and then he can't help glancing at the door where the grey horse stands.

Outside, Beregost is fully awake. Hammers ring up and down the street out of time with each other. Coal smoke hangs low over the roofs, and a cart of charcoal is backing into a forge yard with a great deal of advice from both ends. Garrick unties the grey. The saddlebags are still buckled the way they were, and Tobin has done his job. Garrick leads the horse by the bridle instead of riding. They walk south down the Way together, the old sergeant's uneven step beside James's silent one, and the cat runs ahead along the edge of a water trough.

The chandler's is a narrow shop smelling of tallow, with bundles of dipped candles hung in the window like onions. Behind it a gate of grey planks stands half open in a yard wall. It's a quarter of an hour's walk from the inn.

Inside, the yard is beaten earth with a long shed down one side. Three wagons stand in a row under the shed roof with their tilts rolled back. Two are loaded nearly to the boards and the third is half done. A pair of men are swinging small casks up into it, salt by the white crust on the staves. Beside the gate, at a trestle with a ledger open on it and a stone on each page against the wind, stands a thin young man of about twenty. He has ink on two fingers and a pen behind his ear. He looks up at the horse, then at Garrick, and then at James and his cloak. He looks longest at the cat, who has already jumped onto the end of the trestle and sat down on the corner of his ledger.

"Sergeant." He puts a finger on the page as if the cat might carry it off. "Master Quell's not in till the second bell. Is this—" He stops, and doesn't quite know how to finish.

"The scout," Garrick says. "Master Worgen. He wants to see the wagons, the load and the men. Show him what he asks for, Ambry."

The two loaders have stopped with a cask between them and are watching.

 *(Out of game: I'll spell the Insight check out more plainly. I don't want it to read as a reaction.)*

James set out to read Sergeant Venn and couldn't. He looked for the small giveaways a card player waits for: the jaw tightening, the blink coming too late, the eyes going somewhere they shouldn't. Garrick showed none of them. He'd spent thirty years standing still while officers shouted in his face, and his face gave nothing away. James walked out of the Anvil and Ember knowing no more than when he sat down. The hand stays on the cup, the man keeps quiet, and one of the seven might have been his, or might not.

opening.text:
Grey light slips through the shutters of a narrow room above the Anvil and Ember. Somewhere down the street a hammer strikes iron, then another and another, until all Beregost seems to be ringing; farther off, a temple bell greets the dawn. The cat is already up, sitting on the windowsill with its tail curled around its paws, watching something below. The purse is where you left it, heavy with about 350 gold, and beside it lies the worn deck of cards.

A knock. The door opens a hand's width and a freckled boy of about twelve edges in with a steaming jug. "Hot water, sir. Ma says breakfast's porridge and sausage, two coppers." He sets the jug on the washstand, glances at the cat, then lingers by the door. "And, um — there's a man downstairs. Been there since first light. He asked if the soldier with the cat was awake yet. Didn't say his name. Didn't order anything, neither." He shifts from foot to foot. "Should I tell him you're up, sir?"
